events.title: Antoninus forces the deification of Hadrian and becomes Pius
events.summary: Hadrian died hated by the Senate, which wanted to annul his acts and refuse him divine honours; Antoninus insisted, arguing that otherwise his own adoption would be void, and secured Hadrian's consecration, earning, by most accounts, the name Pius.
events.detail: Other explanations of the cognomen in the Historia Augusta include his supporting his aged father-in-law in the Senate, saving men Hadrian had condemned in his last illness, and his honours for Hadrian. Antoninus completed the Mausoleum, founded games at Puteoli where Hadrian was first buried, and dedicated a temple of Divus Hadrianus (145). The episode set the tone of a reign built on reconciliation and continuity.

events.title: Lollius Urbicus reconquers southern Scotland
events.summary: Soon after his accession Antoninus sent Quintus Lollius Urbicus to Britain; by 142 he had defeated the peoples of the Lowlands, rebuilt Corbridge as a supply base, and begun the Antonine Wall, and Antoninus took his only imperatorial acclamation (IMP II) for the victory.
events.detail: Inscriptions from Corbridge (139 and 140) record building by II Augusta under Urbicus. Coins of 143-144 show Britannia seated on a rock. The motive for advancing beyond Hadrian's Wall is debated: genuine pressure from the Selgovae and others, or the new emperor's need for military prestige, as Fronto implied.

events.title: Marcus Aurelius named Caesar
events.summary: In 139 the eighteen-year-old Marcus, adopted by Antoninus in 138 under Hadrian's terms, was named Caesar, made quaestor and given residence in the House of Tiberius on the Palatine; his betrothal to Lucius Commodus's sister was broken off in favour of Antoninus's daughter Faustina.
events.detail: Marcus was designated consul for 140 at eighteen. His education under Fronto (Latin rhetoric), Herodes Atticus (Greek) and the Stoic Junius Rusticus is recorded with gratitude in Meditations Book 1. Lucius, the other adoptee, was given no title until 161.

events.title: Temple of Divine Faustina in the Forum
events.summary: After the death of Faustina the Elder in late 140, Antoninus built her a temple on the Sacra Via in 141; after his own death in 161 the Senate added his name, and the inscription still reads DIVO ANTONINO ET DIVAE FAUSTINAE EX S C.
events.detail: The cipollino columns of the pronaos stand to their full height because the temple became the church of San Lorenzo in Miranda (by the 11th century); grooves cut high on the columns show where medieval builders tried to pull them down. The frieze shows griffins and candelabra.

events.title: "Rex Quadis datus": client kings given to the Quadi and Armenia
events.summary: Bronze coins of c. 140-144 show Antoninus crowning a king with the legend REX QVADIS DATVS, and others REX ARMENIIS DATVS, advertising the emperor's right to appoint client rulers beyond the frontier.
events.detail: Antoninus's reign was the high point of Roman diplomatic prestige: the Historia Augusta says kings of the Bactrians, Indians and Hyrcanians sent envoys, that he deterred a Parthian invasion of Armenia by letter alone, and that Pharasmanes II of Iberia visited Rome and was allowed to sacrifice on the Capitol, his equestrian statue set up in the temple of Bellona.
events.locName: Quadi territory north of the Danube

events.title: Earthquake in Rhodes and Lycia
events.summary: A great earthquake around 141-142 struck Rhodes, Lycia and Caria; Antoninus funded reconstruction, and the Lycian millionaire Opramoas of Rhodiapolis gave huge sums to some thirty cities, as recorded on the walls of his tomb in a dossier of letters from the emperor and governors.
events.detail: Pausanias (8.43.4) and the Historia Augusta mention Antoninus's aid to Rhodes and the cities of Asia. Aelius Aristides' Rhodian oration describes the ruined city. The Opramoas inscription, with some seventy documents, is a key text for euergetism and imperial correspondence in the provinces.

events.title: Fronto's correspondence with Marcus and Lucius
events.summary: Marcus Cornelius Fronto of Cirta, consul in 143 and the leading Latin orator of his day, exchanged letters for some thirty years with his pupils Marcus and Lucius; the letters were rediscovered by Angelo Mai in palimpsests at Milan and the Vatican in 1815 and 1823.
events.detail: They show the young Marcus's affection for his teacher, his daily life at Antoninus's villas (grape harvests, hunting, illness), and his turn from rhetoric to philosophy, which Fronto regretted. Fronto's archaising style (elocutio novella) favoured early Latin authors. The letters to Lucius include material on the Parthian war, and Fronto's Principia Historiae was meant to introduce a history of it.

events.title: Roman garrison on the Farasan islands
events.summary: Latin inscriptions found on the Farasan islands off south-west Arabia record a vexillation of legio II Traiana Fortis and the "Ferresani portus" in 144, the most remote Roman garrison known, guarding the Red Sea route to India.
events.detail: The inscriptions, published in 2004-2007, revealed a Roman naval and military presence at the mouth of the Red Sea far beyond the provincial frontiers, probably under the prefect of Mount Berenice and linked to protection of the Indian Ocean trade against piracy.

events.title: Marcus marries Faustina the Younger
events.summary: In April 145 Marcus married his cousin Faustina, Antoninus's only surviving child; after the birth of their first child in late 147 Marcus received tribunician power and proconsular imperium and Faustina the title Augusta.
events.detail: The marriage produced at least fourteen children, including twins born in 161 (Commodus and Titus Aurelius Fulvus Antoninus); only Commodus among the sons survived to adulthood. Coins celebrate Faustina's fertility (FECVNDITAS, TEMPORVM FELICITAS). The hostile tradition that she was unfaithful with gladiators and sailors is generally dismissed.

events.title: Temple of Divus Hadrianus dedicated
events.summary: In 145 Antoninus dedicated the temple of the deified Hadrian in the Campus Martius, whose eleven marble columns survive embedded in the facade of the former Rome stock exchange in the Piazza di Pietra.
events.detail: Reliefs from its precinct, depicting personified provinces alternating with trophies, are now in the Capitoline Museums and Palazzo Massimo; they reflect Hadrian's ideology of an empire of partner provinces rather than conquered peoples.

events.title: Celebrations of Rome's 900th year
events.summary: In 147-148 Antoninus marked the 900th anniversary of Rome's foundation with games and a coinage reviving the city's founding legends: Aeneas carrying Anchises, the wolf and twins, Mars and Rhea Silvia, the sow of Lavinium and Romulus.
events.detail: The Aurelius Victor tradition says Antoninus celebrated the 900th year with splendour. The legend-types, unusually antiquarian, form a coherent series struck mostly in 140-144 and around 148. They fit his promotion of Lanuvium (his birthplace) and of Italian religion and Rome's Trojan heritage.

events.title: Fires, floods and famine under Antoninus Pius
events.summary: The Historia Augusta lists the misfortunes of Antoninus's reign: a famine, the collapse of the Circus Maximus, an earthquake in Rhodes and Asia, a fire in Rome that destroyed 340 apartment blocks and houses, fires at Narbo, Antioch and Carthage, and a Tiber flood, all relieved from imperial funds.
events.detail: The collapse in the Circus during games killed 1,112 people according to the Chronograph of 354. Antoninus is said to have relieved the famine by distributing wine, oil and wheat bought at his own expense. The forum of Carthage was rebuilt with his help; the Antonine Baths there were completed in 162.

events.title: The Muziris papyrus
events.summary: A papyrus in Vienna (P. Vindob. G 40822) of the mid-second century contains a maritime loan agreement for a voyage to Muziris on the Malabar coast and, on its back, the valuation of the cargo of the ship Hermapollon: some 700 to 1,100 talents' worth of nard, ivory and textiles, enough to buy a large estate in Egypt.
events.detail: The 25% customs duty (tetarte) payable at Alexandria on the cargo would alone have exceeded the annual pay of a legion. The text shows the immense scale of individual ventures in the Indian trade and the financing of merchants by lenders. Muziris itself is probably the site at Pattanam in Kerala.

events.title: Valentinus and the Gnostic schools in Rome
events.summary: The Alexandrian Christian teacher Valentinus was active in Rome c. 136-160, developing an elaborate cosmology of divine emanations (aeons) and a myth of Sophia's fall, and nearly became bishop according to Tertullian; his followers Ptolemy and Heracleon founded the most influential "Gnostic" school.
events.detail: Rome in the 140s was home to rival Christian teachers, including Marcion, Valentinus, Cerdo and Justin. The Gospel of Truth found at Nag Hammadi (1945) may be by Valentinus. Irenaeus's Against Heresies (c. 180) was written chiefly against the Valentinians, and the reaction to such teachers shaped the idea of orthodoxy, the canon and episcopal succession.

events.title: Trouble in northern Britain c. 154-158
events.summary: Pausanias says Antoninus deprived the Brigantes of much of their land because they had attacked the Genounian district, subjects of Rome; coins of 154-155 show a dejected Britannia, and the governor Gnaeus Julius Verus brought reinforcements from the German legions c. 155-158.
events.detail: An inscription from the Tyne at Newcastle records the arrival of detachments from the three British legions from the two Germanies under Julius Verus. Earlier views of a major northern revolt that destroyed the Antonine Wall forts have been toned down; the Genounians may not even be British. The episode is linked to the reoccupation of Hadrian's Wall c. 158 and the abandonment of the Antonine Wall in the 160s.
events.debate: Location of the Genounians and scale of the trouble.

events.title: Polycarp and Anicetus disagree on the date of Easter
events.summary: Around 154-155 the aged bishop Polycarp of Smyrna visited Bishop Anicetus of Rome; they failed to agree whether Easter should be kept on the 14th of Nisan whatever the weekday, as Asia did, or on the following Sunday, as at Rome, but parted in peace, Anicetus letting Polycarp celebrate the Eucharist.
events.detail: Irenaeus recalled the meeting in a letter to Victor of Rome during the more bitter Quartodeciman controversy c. 190. Polycarp also met Marcion in Rome and called him "the firstborn of Satan". The visit shortly preceded Polycarp's martyrdom.

sources.w: Letter to Victor (in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 5.24.14-17)

events.title: The outer limes in Upper Germany and Raetia
events.summary: Around 155-160 the Upper German frontier was moved forward up to 30 km from the Neckar-Odenwald line to a new, ruler-straight line from Miltenberg to Lorch, running some 80 km almost without deviation, with stone forts at Osterburken, Jagsthausen and elsewhere.
events.detail: The advance added fertile land to the province and shortened communications to Raetia. Dendrochronology and building inscriptions date the new forts to c. 159-161. The palisade, ditch and bank (Pfahlgraben) and stone towers made this the classic image of the limes, now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

events.title: Antoninus Pius's rescripts on slaves
events.summary: Antoninus ruled that a master who killed his own slave without cause was as liable as if he had killed another's, and that slaves who fled to the statues of the emperor because of intolerable cruelty must be sold to new owners, as in the case of the slaves of Julius Sabinus in Baetica.
events.detail: Gaius (1.53) and the Digest (1.6.2) quote the rescript to the proconsul of Baetica Aelius Marcianus, which states that "it is in the master's interest that relief against cruelty, hunger or intolerable injury should not be denied to those who justly appeal". Antoninus also favoured the presumption in favour of liberty (favor libertatis) in manumission cases. The measures tempered but did not challenge slavery.

events.title: Apuleius tried for magic at Sabratha
events.summary: Around 158-159 the philosopher and orator Apuleius of Madauros was tried before the proconsul Claudius Maximus at Sabratha on a charge of winning the rich widow Pudentilla by magic; his defence speech, the Apology, survives and he was acquitted.
events.detail: The accusers, Pudentilla's relatives, cited his purchase of fish, a wooden statuette he worshipped and his handsomeness. The speech is a showpiece of learned wit and a unique document of a provincial elite feud. Apuleius later wrote the Metamorphoses (The Golden Ass), the only Latin novel to survive complete, with the tale of Cupid and Psyche and a final conversion to Isis, and became priest of the provincial cult at Carthage.

events.title: Rise of Montanism in Phrygia
events.summary: Around 156-172 (dates vary) the Phrygian convert Montanus and the prophetesses Prisca and Maximilla began to prophesy in ecstatic trances, proclaiming the outpouring of the Paraclete and a new Jerusalem at Pepuza; the "New Prophecy" spread to Rome and Carthage, where it won Tertullian.
events.detail: Opponents in Asia held synods against it, among the earliest known. The movement demanded rigorous fasting, forbade second marriage and welcomed martyrdom. The site of Pepuza was identified in 2001 near Karayakuplu in western Turkey. Montanist communities survived in Phrygia until the sixth century.

events.title: Pausanias's Description of Greece
events.summary: Between about 155 and 180 Pausanias, a Greek from Lydia, wrote a ten-book guide to the sanctuaries, monuments, art and local legends of mainland Greece, the indispensable source for archaeologists at Olympia, Delphi, Athens and elsewhere.
events.detail: Datable references include the Odeion of Herodes Atticus (after 161) and the Costoboci raid (170). Pausanias focuses on the ancient and sacred and largely ignores Roman buildings, reflecting the Second Sophistic's classicism. Excavations have repeatedly confirmed his accuracy, from the Olympia Heraion to the tombs at Mycenae.

events.title: Appian's Roman History
events.summary: Appian of Alexandria, an advocate who secured through Fronto a procuratorship from Antoninus, wrote in Greek a history of Rome's wars arranged by region and enemy, culminating in the five books of the Civil Wars, our fullest narrative from the Gracchi to Sextus Pompey.
events.detail: He had witnessed the Jewish revolt in Egypt in 116-117 and escaped by boat. His regional plan (Iberian, Hannibalic, Libyan, Syrian, Mithridatic) preserves sources otherwise lost. A letter of Fronto to Antoninus asking a procuratorship for the elderly Appian survives.

events.title: Tiber flood and famine at the start of Marcus's reign
events.summary: Soon after the joint accession a great Tiber flood in 162 destroyed buildings and many animals in the city and countryside and caused a severe famine, relieved by the emperors in person.
events.detail: The Historia Augusta lists it among the calamities of the opening years: war with Parthia, unrest in Britain, the Chatti invading Germany and Raetia. Marcus appointed curators for the affected communities. The disasters foreshadowed the plague that arrived four years later.

events.title: The Chatti invade Upper Germany and Raetia
events.summary: In 162 the Chatti broke into Upper Germany and Raetia; Gaius Aufidius Victorinus, Fronto's son-in-law, was sent to repel them, while the Britons were also restless and Calpurnius Agricola was sent against them.
events.detail: The attacks were early signs of pressure on the northern frontiers that culminated after 166. The Chatti appear again in 213 under Caracalla.

events.title: Galen arrives in Rome
events.summary: In 162 the 33-year-old Galen of Pergamum, former physician to the gladiators of the high priest of Asia, came to Rome, where his public anatomical demonstrations, including vivisection of pigs to show the role of the recurrent laryngeal nerve in the voice, made him famous and controversial.
events.detail: He treated the philosopher Eudemus and the consul Flavius Boethus, for whom he wrote anatomical works. In 166, as the plague reached Rome, he left for Pergamum, claiming enemies; in 168-169 the emperors summoned him to Aquileia, and he became physician to the young Commodus. His some 150 surviving works, a tenth of ancient Greek literature, dominated medicine until the seventeenth century. The rediscovered treatise On Avoiding Distress (2005) describes his losses in the Palatine fire of 192.

events.title: Lucius Verus marries Lucilla at Ephesus
events.summary: In 164 Marcus escorted his daughter Lucilla, aged about fourteen, as far as Brundisium, and Lucius left the front to marry her at Ephesus, where she became Augusta.
events.detail: Marcus turned back to avoid seeming to seek a share in the glory of the war, and also, the Historia Augusta suggests, to keep an eye on rumours of Lucius's debaucheries at Antioch and Daphne. After Lucius's death in 169 Lucilla was married against her will to the older general Claudius Pompeianus; she later led the conspiracy of 182 against her brother.

events.title: Sohaemus installed as king of Armenia
events.summary: After Statius Priscus took Artaxata in 163, Rome built a new capital at Kainepolis (Vagharshapat) and installed Sohaemus, an Arsacid-Emesene prince and Roman senator, as king of Armenia; coins of 164 show Lucius giving him the crown with the legend REX ARMENIIS DATVS.
events.detail: Lucius took the title Armeniacus. Sohaemus, a member of the Emesene royal house, was later expelled by a pro-Parthian faction c. 172 and restored by Martius Verus. Kainepolis, garrisoned by Roman troops, became the nucleus of Etchmiadzin.

events.title: Romans take Edessa, Nisibis and Dura-Europos
events.summary: In 165 Roman columns under Avidius Cassius advanced down the Euphrates, winning a battle at Europos (Dura) and taking the city, while Martius Verus captured Edessa and restored the pro-Roman king Mannus; Nisibis also fell.
events.detail: Dura-Europos remained a Roman garrison town until its destruction by the Sasanians c. 256, preserving its synagogue, church house and military archives. Lucian mocks historians who invented bloody battles for the war, including one at Europos with 70,236 enemy dead. Coins of Mannus of Edessa carry Roman imperial portraits.

events.title: Lucian's How to Write History
events.summary: Lucian of Samosata wrote How to Write History c. 166, satirising the flood of flattering histories of Lucius Verus's Parthian war, which invented battles, borrowed from Thucydides and made Roman generals into Achilles.
events.detail: The essay lays down principles still quoted: the historian should be fearless, incorruptible, "a stranger in his books and without a country". Lucian's other works, some 80 in all, include the True Histories (a parody travel tale reaching the moon), Alexander the False Prophet, The Passing of Peregrinus (on a Cynic who burned himself at Olympia in 165, with an early pagan comment on Christians) and dialogues of the gods and the dead.

events.title: Avidius Cassius invades Media
events.summary: In 166 Avidius Cassius crossed the Tigris and invaded Media, earning Lucius and Marcus the title Medicus; but the plague, said to have broken out in Seleucia, spread through the army, which returned to Syria.
events.detail: The war ended with Roman control of north-western Mesopotamia (Dura, Carrhae, Edessa as client) and Cassius given a supra-provincial command in the East, the base of his usurpation in 175. Lucius returned to Rome for the joint triumph of October 166.

events.title: Roman "embassy" reaches the Han court
events.summary: The Book of the Later Han records that in 166 an embassy from Andun (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus), king of Da Qin (the Roman empire), arrived from beyond Rinan (Vietnam) and presented ivory, rhinoceros horn and tortoiseshell, the first direct contact recorded between Rome and China.
events.detail: The Chinese account notes that the gifts were unremarkable, suspecting that the envoys were merchants who had acquired them on the way rather than official ambassadors. Earlier, the Han general Ban Chao's envoy Gan Ying had reached the Persian Gulf in 97 but turned back. Roman coins and glass found at Oc Eo in the Mekong delta attest the southern sea route.
events.debate: Probably merchants claiming embassy status rather than an official mission.

events.title: The Antonine Plague reaches Rome
events.summary: Brought back by Verus's army, the plague reached Rome in 166, killing thousands; the Historia Augusta says that corpses were carried away in carts, and that Marcus buried the poor at public expense and issued laws on burial.
events.detail: Galen left Rome that year. Later traditions blamed the soldiers who had opened a golden casket in the temple of Apollo at Seleucia. The disease, from Galen's description of fever, black rash and black stools, was probably smallpox. It returned in waves for some twenty years.

events.title: Alexander of Abonoteichus and the plague oracle
events.summary: The prophet Alexander of Abonoteichus, founder of the oracle of the human-headed snake god Glykon, issued during the plague a one-line verse oracle, "Phoebus the unshorn keeps off the cloud of plague", which was inscribed over doorways, ironically, Lucian says, the houses so marked suffering worst.
events.detail: Lucian's Alexander the False Prophet is a hostile exposé; Alexander nevertheless won the patronage of the consular Rutilianus and sent an oracle to Marcus during the Marcomannic war advising him to throw two lions into the Danube, after which the Romans were defeated. Coins of Abonoteichus (renamed Ionopolis) and statuettes of Glykon confirm the cult's popularity.

events.title: Martyrdom of Justin and his companions
events.summary: Around 165 the Christian philosopher Justin and six companions were tried before the urban prefect Quintus Junius Rusticus, Marcus Aurelius's Stoic teacher, refused to sacrifice and were beheaded; the Acts of their martyrdom preserve the interrogation.
events.detail: Justin, from Flavia Neapolis in Samaria, had taught in Rome "above the baths of Myrtinus". Eusebius reports that the Cynic Crescens, whom Justin had bested in debate, denounced him. The Acts are among the most reliable early martyr texts, showing the routine procedure under which confession of the name sufficed for death.

events.title: Marcus and Lucius set out for the northern front
events.summary: In spring 168 both emperors left Rome for Aquileia to meet the barbarian incursions; the Marcomanni and Victuali sought terms, the praetorian prefect Furius Victorinus died of plague, and the army was ravaged by disease in the winter of 168/169.
events.detail: Galen, summoned to Aquileia, says the plague raged as never before and the emperors fled to Rome with a few soldiers, Lucius dying on the way early in 169. Marcus purified the city with every rite and recruited slaves, gladiators, Dalmatian brigands and German mercenaries to fill the ranks.

events.title: The three Dacias under one consular legate
events.summary: Around 168 Marcus united the three Dacian provinces (Porolissensis, Apulensis, Malvensis) under a consular legate, Marcus Claudius Fronto, who also held Moesia Superior; he was killed fighting Germans and Iazyges in 170.
events.detail: An inscription in the Forum of Trajan honours Fronto, who "fell fighting bravely for the state". Legio V Macedonica was moved to Potaissa to give Dacia a second legion. The province was briefly overrun by Iazyges and Astingi; the gold-mining tablets at Alburnus Maior stop in 167, perhaps from abandonment in the invasion.

events.title: Debasement of the denarius under Marcus and Commodus
events.summary: Under the fiscal strain of the plague and the northern wars the silver content of the denarius fell from about 83% under Antoninus Pius to about 75-79% by the late years of Marcus, and somewhat further under Commodus, who also lowered its weight.
events.detail: Metallurgical analyses (Walker, Butcher and Ponting) show stepwise reductions rather than collapse; the real crash came under Septimius Severus, when fineness fell to around 50%. Marcus's auction of palace treasures in 169 and his refusal of a donative after victories reflect the same pressures.
events.debate: Exact percentages vary with analytical method and sample.

events.title: Astingi and Lacringi on the Dacian frontier
events.summary: In 171 the Vandal Astingi under their kings Raus and Raptus came to Dacia seeking land in return for alliance; the governor Sextus Cornelius Clemens set them against the Costoboci, but the Lacringi, fearing their presence, attacked them, and the Astingi became Roman allies.
events.detail: Dio's account is the earliest mention of Vandal groups in contact with Rome. The episode shows the divide-and-rule diplomacy that accompanied fighting in the Marcomannic wars, as migrating peoples pressed on the Danube from the north.

events.title: Marcus at Carnuntum: invaders expelled from Italy and Noricum
events.summary: In 171 Marcus established his headquarters at Carnuntum; Claudius Pompeianus and Pertinax cleared the invaders from Italy and Noricum, destroying Marcomannic war bands as they recrossed the Danube with booty, and Marcus received embassies from peoples seeking alliance or terms.
events.detail: Dio says some peoples were granted land in Dacia, Pannonia, Moesia and Germany or even Italy, and the Quadi made a separate peace, returning 13,000 prisoners. Book 2 of the Meditations is headed "at Carnuntum". Pertinax's success restored a career that had stalled.

events.title: Marcus defeats the Marcomanni; title Germanicus
events.summary: In 172 Marcus crossed the Danube into the Marcomannic lands, winning victories that earned him and Commodus the title Germanicus and coins proclaiming GERMANIA SVBACTA, the year also of the "rain miracle" and, according to coins and the column, a lightning miracle that destroyed an enemy siege engine.
events.detail: Roman camps at Musov (Burgstall) in Moravia, with legionary detachments and a forward command post, date from the Marcomannic wars. The Column of Marcus Aurelius shows the river crossing on a pontoon bridge at its base and divine interventions in the early scenes.

events.title: The Chauci raid Gallia Belgica
events.summary: Around 172 the Chauci raided the coast of Gallia Belgica; the governor Didius Julianus, the future emperor, defeated them with hastily levied provincial troops.
events.detail: Coin hoards and burned villas in northern Gaul from the 170s have been connected with the raids, though their scale is uncertain. The episode foreshadows the seaborne Frankish and Saxon raids of the third century.

events.title: The Quadi depose Furtius; Marcus puts a price on Ariogaesus
events.summary: In 174 the Quadi expelled their Roman-approved king Furtius and chose Ariogaesus; Marcus refused to recognise him and offered 1,000 gold pieces to anyone who brought him alive and 500 for his head, and when Ariogaesus was captured, exiled him to Alexandria.
events.detail: The Quadi had broken their peace by sheltering Marcomannic fugitives and refusing to return deserters. The Laugaricio inscription at Trencin records a legionary detachment wintering 120 km north of the Danube in 179-180. Book 1 of the Meditations ends "among the Quadi, on the Granua" (Hron).

events.title: Death of Faustina the Younger at Halala
events.summary: Accompanying Marcus to the East after Avidius Cassius's revolt, Faustina, "Mother of the Camps" (mater castrorum) since 174, died in winter 175/176 at Halala in the Taurus foothills, which Marcus refounded as the colony Faustinopolis.
events.detail: Dio reports the rumour that she had encouraged Cassius, believing Marcus near death, and killed herself to avoid exposure; modern scholars are sceptical. Marcus had her deified, founded a second order of puellae Faustinianae, and placed silver statues of her and himself in the temple of Venus and Roma, where newly married couples sacrificed.

events.title: Marcus's tour of the East after Cassius's revolt
events.summary: In 175-176 Marcus, with Commodus, toured Syria, Egypt and Asia; he burned Cassius's correspondence unread, pardoned most supporters, punished Antioch by suspending its games and assemblies, behaved at Alexandria as a citizen and philosopher, and at Smyrna heard Aelius Aristides declaim.
events.detail: He also forbade anyone to govern his province of origin, because Cassius was a Syrian. Aristides made Marcus wait three days before speaking, according to Philostratus. The tour ended at Athens with the initiation and the endowment of the chairs.

events.title: Tabula Banasitana: citizenship for a Moorish chief
events.summary: A bronze tablet found at Banasa in 1957 records grants of Roman citizenship in 168/169 and 177 by Marcus (and Commodus) to Julianus of the Zegrenses, a Moorish tribal leader, and his family, "salvo iure gentis", without prejudice to their tribal law or the taxes due to the fisc.
events.detail: The documents include letters from the emperors to the governors of Tingitana and an extract from the imperial register (commentarius) of citizenship grants, with the signatures of twelve members of the emperor's council. The formula "salvo iure gentis" shows that holding citizenship did not cancel local obligations, which bears on the interpretation of the Constitutio Antoniniana of 212.

events.title: Celsus writes the True Doctrine against the Christians
events.summary: Around 175-180 the Platonist Celsus wrote the Alethes Logos, the first known systematic pagan attack on Christianity, mocking its appeal to the uneducated, its claims about Jesus's birth and resurrection and its refusal to serve the state.
events.detail: The work survives only through Origen's point-by-point reply Contra Celsum (c. 248), which quotes perhaps 70% of it. Celsus knew the gospels, Jewish anti-Christian polemic (including the story that Jesus's father was a soldier named Panthera) and the variety of Christian sects. He closes by urging Christians to take part in civic life and fight for the emperor.

events.title: Earthquake destroys Smyrna
events.summary: A violent earthquake levelled Smyrna in 177 or 178; Aelius Aristides wrote a letter to Marcus and Commodus so moving that, according to Philostratus, Marcus wept over it and promised to rebuild the city.
events.detail: Aristides' Smyrnaean Orations (18-21) lament and celebrate the city. The rebuilding, financed by the emperors and funded by remitted taxes, was celebrated by Aristides as Smyrna's rebirth; the excavated Agora of Smyrna (Izmir) belongs largely to this Marcan reconstruction, with a portrait of Faustina on its arch.

events.title: Senatus consultum Orfitianum
events.summary: A decree of the Senate of 178, proposed by Marcus and Commodus in the consulship of Orfitus, gave children priority over the agnatic relatives in inheriting from their mother on intestacy.
events.detail: With the Hadrianic SC Tertullianum (mother inheriting from children), it marked a decisive step from the old agnatic family, based on descent through males under paternal power, towards a cognatic system based on blood relationship. Justinian's reforms of succession built on both decrees.

events.title: Marcus and Commodus leave for the second German expedition
events.summary: On 3 August 178 Marcus and Commodus left Rome for the Danube after Marcus, acting as fetial priest, hurled a bloody spear from the temple of Bellona into "enemy territory", reviving an ancient rite of declaring war.
events.detail: Dio reports the ritual. The expedition aimed at completing the subjugation of the Marcomanni and Quadi, possibly to create new provinces. Tarrutenius Paternus, praetorian prefect and a writer on military law, held field command.

events.title: Paternus's victory over the Quadi
events.summary: In 179 the praetorian prefect Tarrutenius Paternus fought a day-long battle against the barbarians, probably Quadi, and destroyed their army, earning Marcus his tenth imperatorial acclamation.
events.detail: Dio says the Quadi, unable to endure the garrisons of 20,000 men in forts among them with baths and every comfort, tried to migrate north to the Semnones, but Marcus blocked the roads. The battle is the last recorded engagement of Marcus's reign.

battle.significance: Final Marcan victory; opened the way to annexation that Commodus abandoned.

events.title: Valerius Maximianus kills Valao, king of the Naristi
events.summary: An inscription from Diana Veteranorum (Zana) in Numidia records that Marcus Valerius Maximianus, a cavalry prefect from Poetovio, killed with his own hand Valao, chief of the Naristi, and was rewarded by Marcus with a horse, trappings and weapons.
events.detail: The career inscription is one of the most detailed for the Marcomannic wars: Maximianus brought grain down the Danube for the Pannonian armies, commanded Moorish horsemen against the Germans, led vexillations wintering at Laugaricio and rose to consul and legate of Numidia under Commodus.

events.title: Barbarian settlers in Italy and the revolt at Ravenna
events.summary: Marcus settled surrendered Germans within the empire, including in Italy; when those planted near Ravenna rebelled and tried to seize the city, he expelled all barbarians from Italy and settled them only in the frontier provinces.
events.detail: Dio is the source. Such settlements (receptio) foreshadowed the late Roman practice of accepting barbarian groups as farmers and recruits. The Historia Augusta claims Marcus settled "infinite numbers" on Roman soil, filling lands depopulated by the plague.

events.title: Plans for provinces of Marcomannia and Sarmatia
events.summary: The Historia Augusta says that had Marcus lived another year he would have made the lands of the Marcomanni and Sarmatians into provinces; in 179-180 some 20,000 Roman soldiers were stationed in forts in Marcomannic and Quadic territory.
events.detail: The claim is debated: some see the occupation as a prelude to annexation, others as a security measure. Archaeology north of the Danube (Musov, Iza, Laugaricio) confirms large temporary installations. Commodus withdrew them under the peace of 180, a decision Dio and Herodian blame on his laziness but which many modern historians think prudent.
events.locName: Bohemia, Moravia and the Hungarian plain

events.title: Irenaeus of Lyon writes Against Heresies
events.summary: Around 180 Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon after the martyrdoms of 177, wrote five books of the Refutation and Overthrow of Knowledge Falsely So Called against Valentinian and other Gnostics, arguing from a four-gospel canon and the succession of bishops from the apostles.
events.detail: His list of Roman bishops from Linus to Eleutherus (3.3.3) is the earliest such catalogue, and his insistence that there are exactly four gospels, "as there are four winds", is the first clear statement of the fourfold canon. A native of Asia, he had heard Polycarp in his youth. The full text survives in Latin translation.

events.title: Martyrs of Scilli
events.summary: On 17 July 180 twelve Christians from Scilli in Africa were tried before the proconsul Vigellius Saturninus at Carthage and beheaded; the Acts of their martyrdom are the earliest dated document of Latin Christianity.
events.detail: Asked what was in their case, the leader Speratus replied "books and the letters of Paul, a just man", showing that Latin scriptures existed. Saturninus offered them thirty days to reconsider. Tertullian says this proconsul was the first to use the sword against Christians in Africa.

events.title: Petition of the coloni of the saltus Burunitanus
events.summary: An inscription from Souk el-Khmis in Tunisia records a petition by the tenant farmers of the imperial estate called saltus Burunitanus to Commodus (c. 180-183), complaining that the lessee Allius Maximus, with the procurator's collusion, demanded more than the six days' labour a year allowed by the Hadrianic law and had them beaten; Commodus ordered the law upheld.
events.detail: The tenants describe themselves as "wretched peasants" and threaten to flee. The text shows the relationship between coloni, conductores and procurators on imperial estates, and the emperor's role as a court of appeal for humble petitioners.

events.title: Execution of the Quintilii brothers
events.summary: After the conspiracy of Lucilla, Commodus executed the brothers Sextus Quintilius Condianus and Sextus Quintilius Valerius Maximus, consuls together in 151, inseparable in life and in their joint letters, and the praetorian prefect Tarrutenius Paternus.
events.detail: Their enormous villa on the Via Appia was confiscated and became an imperial residence that Commodus enjoyed. Dio says Condianus's son faked his death by drinking hare's blood and falling from a horse, and a ram was burned in his place, and that many impostors later claimed to be him. Saoterus, Commodus's chamberlain, was killed by the prefects around the same time.
events.locName: Villa of the Quintilii, Via Appia

events.title: War with the free Dacians under Commodus
events.summary: Around 182-183 the free Dacians beyond the province rose and were defeated by commanders including the future rivals Clodius Albinus and Pescennius Niger; Commodus took the title Germanicus Maximus, and the governor Sabinianus settled 12,000 Dacians expelled from their land within the province.
events.detail: Dio records Sabinianus's settlement. The war shows the continued instability north of the Danube after the Marcomannic peace. Victories in Britain under Ulpius Marcellus brought Commodus the title Britannicus in 184.

events.title: Pertinax suppresses a mutiny in Britain
events.summary: Sent to govern Britain after the fall of Perennis, Pertinax faced a mutiny in which a legion tried to proclaim him emperor; he refused, was left for dead in a riot, recovered and punished the mutineers severely, and asked to be recalled because of his unpopularity with the troops.
events.detail: The British army had already sent 1,500 men to Italy in 185 to denounce Perennis. Pertinax's severity in Britain prefigured his attempt to discipline the praetorians in 193, which cost him his life.

events.title: Commodus founds an African grain fleet
events.summary: Around 186 Commodus created a state fleet to carry African grain to Rome, the classis Africana Commodiana Herculea, as a reserve in case the Egyptian grain supply failed.
events.detail: The Historia Augusta, hostile as always, mocks him for naming Carthage after himself (Alexandria Commodiana Togata) and calling the fleet Commodiana Herculea. The measure foreshadows the growing role of African grain, which became Rome's principal supply after Constantinople took the Egyptian annona in 330. Shortages in 189-190 nonetheless led to the riot that brought down Cleander.

events.title: Return of the plague: 2,000 deaths a day in Rome
events.summary: In 189 the plague returned in the worst outbreak Dio, then a senator in Rome, ever knew, with 2,000 people often dying in a single day; Commodus withdrew to Laurentum, where the laurel groves were thought to protect against infection.
events.detail: Dio also reports that criminals spread the disease by pricking people with needles smeared with poison, a typical plague panic. The outbreak combined with famine to produce the riot of 190 against Cleander. Herodian describes similar mortality among people and animals.

events.title: The death of Julius Alexander of Emesa
events.summary: Around 189-190 Commodus sent assassins against Julius Alexander of Emesa, a noble who had killed a lion with a javelin from horseback; Alexander killed them, fled towards Parthia with a favourite boy, and when overtaken killed the boy and himself.
events.detail: Dio tells the story as an example of Commodus's jealousy of anyone excelling in his own pursuits. The episode belongs to the last violent years of the reign; Commodus himself would display his skill as a beast-fighter in the arena in 192.

events.title: Marcia secures the release of Christians from the Sardinian mines
events.summary: Around 190 Commodus's mistress Marcia, who favoured the Christians, obtained from Bishop Victor of Rome a list of confessors condemned to the mines of Sardinia and secured their release through the presbyter Hyacinthus; among them was the future pope Callistus.
events.detail: The story comes from Hippolytus's hostile account of Callistus, a former slave of the imperial freedman Carpophorus, condemned for brawling in a synagogue. Marcia's Christian sympathies (Dio calls her favourable to Christians) illustrate the penetration of the faith into the imperial household by the late second century.

events.title: Victor of Rome and the Quartodeciman controversy
events.summary: Around 190 Bishop Victor of Rome demanded that the churches of Asia abandon their custom of celebrating Easter on 14 Nisan and threatened to excommunicate them; Polycrates of Ephesus refused, citing apostolic tradition, and Irenaeus urged Victor to keep peace as his predecessors had.
events.detail: Eusebius reports synods in Palestine, Rome, Pontus, Gaul and Osrhoene that all supported Sunday observance. The episode is the first major assertion of Roman authority over other churches, and the first Latin-speaking bishop of Rome (Victor was African). The question was settled for most churches at Nicaea in 325.
